english: doing one thing and then switching mid-action (and in the middle...)
formNote: Attach -다가 straight onto any verb stem with no sound change (가다 → 가다가, 먹다 → 먹다가, 일하다 → 일하다가). It means you were doing one action and then stopped or switched to another partway through, so the first action is left unfinished. In casual speech the 가 is often dropped to just -다 (집에 가다 길 잃었어). For an action that fully finished before the next, use -고 나서 instead.
usage: I woke up in the middle of sleeping
I fell asleep while watching TV
examples: 퇴근하다가 마트 들러서 장 봤어요.
On my way home from work I stopped by the mart and got groceries.
퇴근하다 = leave work; 장 보다 = grocery-shop
넷플릭스 보다가 그냥 잠들어 버렸어.
I was watching Netflix and just ended up falling asleep.
Casual; pairs naturally with -아/어 버리다
걸어가다가 옛날 회사 동료 만났어요.
I ran into an old work colleague while walking.
동료 = coworker; unexpected event mid-action
mistakes: Using -다가 for an action you fully finished first — if you completed eating then left, that's 먹고 나서 나갔어요, not 먹다가 나갔어요 (which means you stopped eating partway).

english: after finishing (and then, once that's done)
formNote: Attach -고 나서 to any verb stem with no sound change (먹다 → 먹고 나서, 끝나다 → 끝나고 나서, 운동하다 → 운동하고 나서). It stresses that the first action is fully completed before the second begins — stronger than plain -고. You can also say -고 나면 (once you've done X, then...) for a conditional version. Only the second clause carries the tense.
usage: I work out after I get off work
examples: 월급 받고 나서 한턱낼게요.
Once I get my paycheck, I'll treat you.
한턱내다 = treat someone; relatable money timing
이사하고 나서 집들이 한번 해야죠.
After moving in, I should throw a housewarming.
집들이 = housewarming party
회의 끝나고 나서 점심 같이 먹어요.
Let's have lunch together after the meeting wraps up.
Office sequence; 회의 = meeting
mistakes: Adding tense to the first clause — it's 밥 먹고 나서, not 밥 먹었고 나서. Only the final verb shows tense.

english: while still in that state / leaving it as it is (without changing it)
formNote: Attach -ㄴ 채로 to vowel-ending stems (켜다 → 켠 채로, 신다 is consonant so 신은 채로) and -은 채로 to consonant-ending stems (입다 → 입은 채로, 앉다 → 앉은 채로). It describes doing something while a prior state is left unchanged — e.g. fell asleep with the lights on. The 로 is often dropped to just -(으)ㄴ 채. It pairs with verbs that leave a lasting state (켜다, 신다, 앉다, 누르다), not ongoing actions.
usage: I slept with the light left on
He came in with his shoes still on
Big faux pas in Korean homes
서다 → 선 채로; state held during another action
I left with the window still open
examples: 어제 화장 안 지운 채로 그냥 잤어요.
I just slept last night without taking my makeup off.
화장 지우다 = remove makeup; common late-night confession
이어폰 낀 채로 자다가 목 아팠어.
I fell asleep with my earbuds in and my neck hurt.
이어폰 끼다 = wear earbuds; casual
에어컨 켠 채로 외출하면 전기세 나와요.
If you go out with the AC left on, the electric bill adds up.
전기세 = electricity bill; practical living tip
mistakes: Using it with action verbs like 먹다 to mean 'while eating' — that's 먹으면서. -(으)ㄴ 채로 is for a held STATE (앉은 채로 = while seated), not an ongoing action.

english: because of (an unexpected, usually bad thing that messed things up)
formNote: Attach -는 바람에 to any verb stem (늦다 → 늦는 바람에, 놓치다 → 놓치는 바람에, 막히다 → 막히는 바람에). Despite the -는 (present-looking) form, it always refers to a past cause, and the result clause is in the past tense. It gives a sudden, unintended reason that led to a negative or surprising outcome, so it often sounds like an excuse. It does not take adjectives.
usage: I was late because of traffic
examples: 알람을 못 듣는 바람에 회사에 지각했어요.
I overslept through my alarm so I was late to work.
지각하다 = be late/tardy; very relatable excuse
앞에서 사고 나는 바람에 두 시간이나 갇혔어.
There was an accident up ahead so I was stuck for two whole hours.
Casual; 갇히다 = get stuck/trapped
서버가 터지는 바람에 일을 다시 했어요.
The server crashed so I had to redo the work.
서버 터지다 = server crashes; office/tech context
mistakes: Using it for good results — 바람에 carries a negative/disruptive nuance, so for a welcome cause use -아서/어서 or -덕분에 (thanks to) instead.

english: it's probably the case that... (but) / I'd guess... so (worry or contrast)
formNote: Attach -ㄹ 텐데 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 올 텐데, 바쁘다 → 바쁠 텐데) and -을 텐데 to consonant-ending stems (힘들다 drops ㄹ → 힘들 텐데, 좋다 → 좋을 텐데). It expresses a strong assumption ('it must/should be...') usually followed by a contrast or worry. For a past guess use -았/었을 텐데 (피곤했을 텐데 = you must've been tired). It often trails off as a soft, caring -ㄹ 텐데(요).
usage: you must be worn out, so rest a bit
you must be hungry, so eat something
곧 올 텐데 왜 안 오지?
they should be here soon — why aren't they?
examples: 야근했으면 피곤할 텐데 내일 일찍 들어가요.
If you worked late you must be tired, so head home early tomorrow.
야근 = overtime; warm coworker tone
주말이라 사람 많을 텐데 예약하고 가자.
It's the weekend so it'll probably be packed — let's book and go.
Casual planning with a contrast
월세도 빠듯할 텐데 무리하지 마세요.
Money must be tight with rent, so don't overdo it.
월세 = monthly rent; considerate advice
mistakes: Confusing it with -ㄹ 건데 (a plan: 'I'm going to, but'). -(으)ㄹ 텐데 is a GUESS about something probable, not your own intention.

english: (I observed X) and then... / used to..., but now... (firsthand change)
formNote: Attach -더니 directly to a verb or adjective stem (그러다 → 그러더니, 아프다 → 아프더니). It links something you personally witnessed in the past to a result or change that followed — like 'he kept coughing, and then he got sick.' The subject is usually someone/something other than 'I.' For your own past habit leading to a present result, use -았/었더니 (많이 먹었더니 배불러 = I ate a lot, so now I'm full).
usage: he kept coughing and then caught a cold
it was cold this morning but now it's warm
I ate a lot so now I'm sleepy
examples: 걔 어제 야식 먹더니 오늘 속 안 좋대.
She had a late-night snack yesterday and now says her stomach's off.
야식 = late-night food; 걔 = that person, casual
신입 때 어리바리하더니 이제 일 진짜 잘해요.
He was clueless as a newbie but now he's really good at the job.
신입 = new hire; observed growth over time
하루 종일 굶었더니 머리가 어지러워요.
I starved all day so now I feel dizzy.
-았더니 = my own action led to this state; 굶다 = skip meals
mistakes: Using plain -더니 about your OWN action — for that use -았/었더니 (내가 무리했더니 = I overdid it, so...). Plain -더니 is mainly for what you observed in someone/something else.

english: since / seeing as (I saw or heard X, so I did Y)
formNote: Attach -길래 directly to a verb or adjective stem (싸다 → 싸길래, 울다 → 울길래, 맛있다 → 맛있길래). It gives a reason based on something you noticed or were told, which then prompted your own action in the response clause — so the second clause is almost always your own choice, usually in the past. For nouns use N(이)길래. It's conversational; the more formal/written equivalent is -기에.
usage: it was cheap so I bought it
it looked good so I ordered it
there was no reply so I called
everyone was going so I went too
examples: 편의점에서 1+1 하길래 두 개 사 왔어요.
It was buy-one-get-one at the convenience store so I grabbed two.
1+1 (원 플러스 원) = BOGO; everyday deal
네가 안 보이길래 먼저 갔지.
You were nowhere to be seen so I went ahead.
Casual; reason for one's own action
리뷰가 좋길래 그 식당 예약했어요.
The reviews were good so I booked that restaurant.
리뷰 = reviews; deciding based on info
mistakes: Using -길래 when the second clause isn't your own reactive action — 'It's cheap so it sells well' is a general fact (싸서 잘 팔려요), not -길래. -길래 leads to what YOU did in response.

english: (it's been some time) since... (how long since an action)
formNote: Attach -ㄴ 지 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 온 지, 만나다 → 만난 지) and -은 지 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹은 지, 살다 drops ㄹ → 산 지). It measures elapsed time since an action and is followed by a duration plus 됐어요/지났어요 (한국에 온 지 1년 됐어요). Write 지 with a space — this time 지 is different from the negative -지 (안). 얼마나 됐어요? asks 'how long has it been?'
usage: it hasn't been long since I came
it's been a year since we met
it's been a while since I ate
how long since you bought it?
examples: 한국에 산 지 이제 막 6개월 됐어요.
I've only just hit six months living in Korea.
Newcomer self-intro; note 살다 → 산 지
걔랑 연락 끊은 지 진짜 오래됐어.
It's been ages since I cut off contact with them.
연락 끊다 = stop contact; casual
이 회사 다닌 지 2년쯤 됐어요.
It's been about two years since I started at this company.
다니다 = attend/commute to; work intro
mistakes: Forgetting the space and confusing it with negative -지 — '온 지 1년' (space, time elapsed) vs '오지 않았어요' (no space, negation). They are different 지.

english: the more (you do/it is) X, the more Y
formNote: Attach -ㄹ수록 to vowel-ending stems (가다 → 갈수록, 보다 → 볼수록) and -을수록 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹을수록, 알다 drops ㄹ → 알수록). It shows that as one thing increases, another changes in proportion. It's very often reinforced by putting -(으)면 on the front: 보면 볼수록 (the more I look). 수록 is written attached, with no space.
usage: more and more (as time goes on)
the more I look, the prettier it is
the more I eat, the sleepier I get
the more I learn, the harder it gets
examples: 한국어는 하면 할수록 재밌는 거 같아요.
The more I do Korean, the more fun it seems to get.
Encouraging learner line
월급은 오를수록 쓸 데도 늘어나더라.
The more your salary goes up, the more places there are to spend it.
Casual money truth; -더라 adds 'I found'
서울은 살수록 정 드는 도시예요.
Seoul is a city you grow more attached to the longer you live there.
정(이) 들다 = grow attached; 살다 → 살수록
mistakes: Writing a space (-ㄹ 수록) or confusing it with -ㄹ 수 있다 — 수록 is one chunk attached to the stem (갈수록), unrelated to the ability 수 있다.

english: even if / even though (hypothetically, no matter what)
formNote: Attach -더라도 directly to a verb or adjective stem (가다 → 가더라도, 힘들다 → 힘들더라도, 늦다 → 늦더라도). It concedes a strong or even unlikely hypothetical — stronger than -아도/어도 — meaning 'even supposing that happens, the result still holds.' For a past supposition use -았/었더라도 (알았더라도 = even if I'd known). For nouns: N(이)더라도. It often pairs with 아무리 (no matter how) up front.
usage: no matter how busy, eat your meals
I'll go even if it rains
come for sure even if you're late
examples: 야근하더라도 마감은 지켜야죠.
Even if it means overtime, we have to make the deadline.
야근 = overtime; 마감 = deadline; work resolve
아무리 피곤하더라도 운동은 빠지지 마.
No matter how tired you are, don't skip your workout.
Casual; firm advice with 아무리
조건이 좋더라도 계약서는 꼼꼼히 봐요.
Even if the terms look good, read the contract carefully.
계약서 = contract; practical living advice
mistakes: Treating it as identical to -아도/어도 — both mean 'even if,' but -더라도 is more hypothetical and emphatic, used for stronger or less likely suppositions ('even supposing...').
